Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

both adjective and pronoun

also both of us, both of them, the two of them, on both sides

classical

Hor. S. 2.8.17: habēmus utrumque
Plin. Ep. 4.1.1: grātum est utrīque nostrum

uterque, utraque, utrumque

pronoun and adjective; gen. utriusque, dat. utrīque; with a singular verb

both, each of the two

Lewis & Short: uterque takes the two one by one, ambō as a pair. With a noun it agrees; with a pronoun it takes a genitive: uterque nostrum, both of us. A plural verb with it is rare in the best prose, never in Cicero (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • ambō, ambae, ambō — both (together, as a pair)

    numeral adjective, declined like duo: dat. and abl. ambōbus, ambābus · also used · classical · Plaut. Rud. 1423: vōs hīc hodiē cēnātōte ambō; Catull. 104.2: ambōbus mihi quae cārior est oculīs

    The masculine accusative is ambō in Cicero, Caesar, Vergil and Horace, who never write ambōs (Lewis & Short); Livy has ambōs (1.55.1).

Examples

  • Albānum … sīve Falernum tē magis adpositīs dēlectat, habēmus utrumque

    if you like Alban or Falernian better than what is on the table, we have bothHor. S. 2.8.16–17

  • grātum est utrīque nostrum quod cupis

    your wish is welcome to both of usPlin. Ep. 4.1.1

  • vōs hīc hodiē cēnātōte ambō. — Fīat.

    you’re both to dine here today. — Done.Plaut. Rud. 1423

  • amplexus ille utrumque et carpēns ōscula dulcemque in ambōs cāritātem partiēns

    he hugged them both, kissing them and sharing his tender love between the twoPhaedr. 3.8.12–13

  • crēdis mē potuisse meae maledīcere vītae, ambōbus mihi quae cārior est oculīs?

    do you think I could have spoken ill of my life, who is dearer to me than both my eyes?Catull. 104.1–2

  • hic quidem ait nōs eandem crisin habēre, quia utrīque dentēs cadunt

    he says that we have reached the same turning point, because both of us are losing our teethSen. Ep. 83.4

See also either, neither, each, two.
